h1: Beer key accounts and on-trade contracts for sales teams
title: Beer Key Accounts and On-Trade Contracts | Craft Beer School
desc: How beer companies manage key on-trade accounts: what goes into a bar or hotel contract, how to measure return on it and what quality terms to include.
teaser: A big bar or hotel group can be worth more than a hundred small outlets. The contract decides whether it pays.
standfirst: Key accounts in beer are the bars, restaurants, hotel groups and pub chains that sell a large share of a brand's on-trade volume. They negotiate hard and expect support. A good contract sets volume, visibility, equipment and quality terms that both sides can measure.
sections: What makes an account a key account

On-trade means places where beer is drunk on the premises: bars, pubs, restaurants, hotels, clubs and taprooms. Off-trade means shops where beer is bought to take away. Key accounts are the on-trade customers that matter most, either for volume, for image or because they influence other outlets. A busy rooftop bar in Bengaluru or a hotel group with outlets across several cities can shape how a brand is seen far beyond its own sales.

Key account management is about a relationship over time rather than a single order. It covers listing, pricing within what regulation allows, menu placement, staff training, draught equipment, events and quality. Our guide to retail execution and outlet audits covers the visit discipline that supports it.
What goes into an on-trade contract

Contracts vary, but common elements include:

  • Listing and range. Which brands and packs the outlet will carry, including any draught taps.
  • Volume commitment. A target or minimum over the contract period.
  • Exclusivity. Whether competing brands are limited in a category or on taps.
  • Support. Equipment such as coolers and draught systems, menus, glassware, staff training and event support.
  • Payment terms and how any support is earned or clawed back if volume falls short.
  • Quality terms. Storage, serving and line cleaning standards.

In India, alcohol advertising is restricted and trade practices are regulated by state rules that vary and change. Contracts need review by the legal and compliance teams in each state.

A key account contract is an investment, so it needs a return calculation. The basic version compares the gross margin earned on the account's volume with the total cost of support: equipment depreciation, service visits, promotional spend and any rebates.

An illustrative case: an outlet commits to 6,000 litres of draught a year. If the brewery's gross margin is ₹100 per litre, the account generates ₹6,00,000 a year. If the draught system, glassware, menus and events cost ₹4,00,000 a year in total, the contribution is ₹2,00,000. If the outlet only pours 4,000 litres, margin falls to ₹4,00,000 and the account breaks even. These figures are invented. The point is that volume shortfalls hit return harder than any other variable, so track volume monthly against the commitment.
Incremental volume is the real test

A strong key account report asks what would have happened without the contract. If the outlet already sold the brand in similar volumes, the contract may have bought loyalty rather than growth. That can still be worth it, especially if a competitor was bidding. It should be measured honestly, though, not reported as new volume.

Compare the account's volume before and after the contract. Then compare it against similar outlets without one. The difference is your best estimate of what the contract really delivered. The same logic applies to promotions, as our guide to trade spend and promotions explains.

Sales teams sometimes leave quality out of contracts because it feels like the outlet's business. It is the brand's business too. A bar that stores kegs in a hot back room, cleans lines rarely or serves beer in greasy glasses delivers a poor version of the brand to every customer.

Simple quality terms help: kegs stored cold and rotated, lines cleaned on a set schedule with a log, serving temperature checked and staff trained to pour. Draught lines are commonly cleaned about every two weeks in good practice. Tie part of the support to these standards so both sides have a reason to keep them.

The best contracts are reviewed, not just renewed. Volumes change, menus change and managers move on. A quarterly review with the account covering volume, quality checks and upcoming events keeps the relationship current. Procurement teams negotiating raw materials face a similar discipline, as our guide on hop contracts shows from the supply side.

Data helps here. Monthly volume by account, draught keg deliveries, quality audit scores and support spend can sit in one simple report. When an account's keg orders drop for two months running, the sales team should know before the contract review, not at it. Often the cause is a change of manager or a competitor's tap going in, both of which a visit can address early.

A first step: list your top ten on-trade accounts with contract volume, actual volume to date and total support cost. Rank them by contribution. The bottom three are where your next negotiation should start.
faqs: What is the on-trade in beer?
Places where beer is drunk on the premises, such as bars, pubs, restaurants, hotels and clubs. The off-trade is shops selling beer to take away.
What does a beer on-trade contract include?
Usually listing and range, volume commitments, any exclusivity, support such as equipment and menus, payment terms and quality standards.
How do you measure return on a key account?
Compare the gross margin on the account's volume with the full cost of support, then check how much volume is truly incremental.
Should quality terms be in a bar contract?
Yes. Storage, line cleaning and serving standards protect the brand. Tying support to them gives both sides a reason to keep them.
